title: Living in the world
hookLine: asked how to get through the world, Nanak points to a lotus and a duck in the water
last: MY SEAT IS THE ONE IN EVERY HEART.

cards: A duck spends its whole day in the pond. It dives for food, paddles against the current. Then it climbs onto the bank, gives one shake, and the water simply isn't there anymore; the feathers underneath are dry.
That small animal answers a serious question in the Sidh Gosht. A yogi named Charpat puts it to Nanak: the world is an ocean, hard to cross, they say, so how does anyone get to the other side?

teach.h: THE LOTUS STAYS. THE DUCK SWIMS.
teach.b: Nanak's reply, in paraphrase: as the lotus stays apart in the water, and as the duck swims in the stream and stays dry, so a person can live.
Earlier on this path the lotus had its day, the flower that rises clean out of the mud. Today, look at the duck, because it does something the lotus doesn't.
A lotus is rooted; it stays put and lets the water move around it. A duck goes places. It hunts, feeds its young, fights the current.
Of the two pictures, the duck is the one with a job. That matters, because the yogis in this poem had answered the world by leaving the household behind, going where the water can't reach.
Nanak doesn't tell them they're wrong to love stillness. He points at a bird completely in the water that comes out dry.

teach.h: NO NEED TO LEAVE THE STREAM.
teach.b: You don't have to leave the stream to stay untouched by it.

teach.h: HOPES ALL AROUND, NOT RULED BY THEM.
teach.b: The same stanza adds a phrase: living with hopes all around and not being ruled by them, keeping the One settled in the mind.
That's the duck's secret said without the bird. The hopes, worries and deadlines are real water; they just don't get under the feathers.
And look where the week has been heading: the last of the ragas, many moods and one Word; a circle on the mountain; the question who are you.
Today's answer gives that self somewhere to live: not a cave, not a peak, but the stream.
In Sikh teaching that picture belongs to the householder, the person with work, a family and bills, who keeps the Name in mind through all of it.

how: Sikhs speak of this stanza when describing the householder's life, grihasti: working, raising a family and serving others while keeping the Name in mind, rather than withdrawing from the world.

games.q: what does “living in the world” mean?
o: a hymn about lotus ponds in the gardens of Punjab
a rule that Sikhs must avoid all worldly work and money
Nanak's answer: like the duck, swim the stream and stay dry

games.q: what's inside the answer — tap the pairs.
p: asks how to cross the world-ocean
rooted, stays apart in the water
swims the stream and stays dry

s: in Nanak's picture, the duck leaves the water to stay dry
it swims in the stream and stays dry; it never leaves the water.
the question behind the picture is how to cross the world-ocean
Charpat asks how anyone gets across the world, an ocean hard to cross.
Nanak tells the yogis they are wrong to love stillness
he doesn't attack their stillness; he points to a bird that is fully in the water and stays dry.

games.q: you're a yogi who believes the only way to stay pure is to leave the world. you ask Nanak how to get across. what does he point to?
o: a cave high on the mountain.
a duck swimming in the stream.
a boat that never touches water.
games.why: he points to the lotus and the duck: fully in the water, and untouched by it.

practice: Bring to mind the busiest stretch waiting for you, the commute, the inbox, the kitchen at dinnertime, and picture yourself right in it, moving and working, then picture the duck paddling hard and the water rolling off its back.
Breathe in: in the stream; breathe out: dry underneath, for a few slow rounds. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath.

wordCard.voice: Living in the world. Nanak's answer to Charpat: like the lotus apart in the water, like the duck that swims the stream and stays dry. Today's word.

orig.note: murgaaee: the water bird in the stanza, swimming in the stream and staying dry.

carryVoice: Your line: the duck stays dry. In the stream all day, and dry underneath. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali, Mahala 1, Sidh Gosht, pauris 4–5, Ang 938 (Charpat's question; the lotus and the duck)
